extracted.intended_audience: employers, workers, commenters, attorneys, and policymakers concerned with the FTC non-compete rule (Part 910)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance used by the FTC to evaluate constitutional objections, requests for exceptions or expansions, and industry- or worker-specific justifications for the Part 910 ban on non-competes. Explains standards, evidentiary expectations, and permissible alternatives the Commission relied on in adopting the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the final rule constitutes a taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether invalidating or banning non-competes by rule effects a constitutional taking requiring compensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission concludes the final rule is not a taking because employers have reasonable alternatives to protect investments; the rule provides an exception for causes of action that accrued before the effective date; States and Federal government have long regulated non-competes; the NPRM provided substantial prior notice (more than 18 months before effective date) and the Commission had explored regulation for years. Prior case-by-case adjudication under section 5 existed. These considerations reduce the likelihood the rule is a compensable taking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process (notice and opportunity to be heard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether applying the final rule to existing non-competes raises due process concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due process minimally requires notice and opportunity to be heard. The Commission considers issuance of an NPRM and notice-and-comment rulemaking to provide sufficient process, and additional process will occur in administrative adjudication or in court before any finding of violation. Due process concerns independent of other constitutional issues (e.g., retroactivity) are addressed by the notice-and-comment procedure and subsequent adjudicative avenues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Good-faith exception (Section 910.3(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception that permits enforcing or attempting to enforce a non-compete or making representations about a non-compete where the actor has a good-faith basis to believe part 910 is inapplicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopted to avoid infringing First Amendment rights and to clarify §910.2(a). The exception applies where an employer has a good-faith belief the rule does not apply. It preserves conduct that is constitutionally protected while still prohibiting misrepresentations absent a good-faith basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noerr-Pennington and sham-lawsuit standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of First Amendment petition protections for litigation and when litigation is an unprotected sham.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under Noerr-Pennington, filing a lawsuit is typically protected even if it tends to restrict competition. However, a suit that is a 'sham' (objectively baseless and subjectively designed solely to prevent competition) is not protected. For non-competes covered by the rule, enforcing or attempting to enforce them would likely be considered a sham; §910.3(b)/(c) ensure the rule does not bar litigation that is actually protected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on representing a worker is subject to a non-compete
rubrics_metrics.description: Rule forbids representing that a worker is subject to a non-compete covered by the rule unless the employer has a good-faith basis to believe the non-compete is enforceable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tied to commercial-speech precedent: government may suppress misleading commercial messages. The rule targets misrepresentations about enforceability; the good-faith exception protects representations that are genuinely protected speech or legitimately believed to be applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for uniform coverage rather than differentiating among workers
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the Commission should apply the rule uniformly to all employers/workers or create carve-outs by industry, occupation, earnings, or other factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission preliminarily concluded uniform application advances objectives better: ensures workers aware of rights, creates certainty, reduces litigation over borderline exceptions. Exceptions increase uncertainty and litigation costs, invite disputes about whether a specific business fits an industry exception, and likely produce in terrorem effects that undermine competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior-executive exception narrowness
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of existing non-competes for senior executives versus other workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final rule allows existing non-competes for senior executives to remain in force but bans new non-competes for all workers. The Commission narrowly defines 'senior executive' in §910.1. A compensation threshold is necessary but not sufficient to define senior executives for this exception; only narrowly defined senior executives qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation by worker compensation or skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether highly paid or highly skilled workers should be excluded from the ban or treated differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission finds non-competes negatively affect highly paid/highly skilled workers by suppressing wages, restricting competitors' access to talent, and restricting entrepreneurship; such workers rarely negotiate meaningful consideration; employers have alternatives. Thus, exclude only narrowly (senior executives), not all highly paid/skilled workers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiation by worker access to trade secrets or confidential information
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether workers who access trade secrets/confidential business information should be exempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission declines exemption: such an exclusion would be unnecessary, unjustified, unworkable, and prone to evasion. Employers overstate the share of workers with such access; less restrictive alternatives (NDAs, tailored protections) exist; broad exceptions would lead to complex fact-specific litigation that creates in terrorem effects undermining the rule's objectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industry-based exceptions (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether industries (e.g., real estate, insurance, financial services, on-air talent, construction, apprenticeships) should be excluded from the rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission carefully considered but declines industry-wide exclusions. Arguments relying on the same justifications (protecting investments, trade secrets, goodwill) do not overcome the finding that non-competes are an unfair method of competition. Industry exceptions would increase uncertainty, litigation, and likely fail to remedy negative competitive effects; less-restrictive alternatives typically suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client- and sales-based industries specific considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that sales/client-based industries (real estate, insurance, IMOs, timeshares) are unique and need non-competes to protect goodwill, leads, or sales methods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission rejects treating worker departure like sale of a business because workers are in unequal bargaining positions and don't receive compensation for leaving. Employer claims about proprietary sales techniques or goodwill can be protected by less-restrictive measures (trade secret law, NDAs); broad non-competes are overbroad and harm competition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Industries with apprenticeships/training (apprenticeship exception)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether industries that invest in long apprenticeships or required training (appraisers, plumbers, veterinarians) should be exempt to protect training investments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission declines to exclude these industries. Employers have less-restrictive alternatives such as fixed-duration contracts; training ROI doesn't justify preventing a worker from working after leaving employer. The final rule may benefit employers by broadening available experienced labor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial-services evidence standard and buy-out argument
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims by financial-services commenters that non-competes are necessary and evidence (studies) that non-competes improve productivity or are harmless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission requires evidence that isolates non-competes' effects; cited studies often concern non-solicitation/NDAs and do not isolate non-competes. Occasional 'buy-outs' do not justify non-competes because they raise competitor costs and create deadweight loss. Firms' pecuniary benefits are not a cognizable justification under section 5 without societal benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-air talent/public-facing talent exception analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether on-air talent requires special protection via non-competes because employers invest in talent reputation and brand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission declines to exempt on-air talent: success is due to both employer investment and worker talent; less-restrictive alternatives (fixed contracts, competing on merits) permit employers to recoup investment. Firms' pecuniary benefits alone are not sufficient to justify an exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction industry claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of construction industry's arguments that non-competes are necessary for innovation and productivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cited studies do not explicitly examine non-competes and do not support exemption. Commission finds final rule will likely improve access to skilled labor and innovation. Less-restrictive alternatives (tailored NDAs, non-solicits) are sufficient to address confidentiality or client concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical-evidence relevance and quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard for evaluating empirical studies submitted in support of exceptions or differentiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies must isolate the effects of non-competes (not conflate with non-solicitation agreements etc.), have appropriate methodology and sample, and demonstrate societal benefits—not just firm pecuniary gains. Conflicting or non-isolating studies carry limited weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of less-restrictive alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether employers have feasible, less-restrictive means to protect legitimate interests (trade secrets, client relationships, training investments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission repeatedly points to NDAs, non-solicitation agreements, fixed-term employment contracts, better pay or terms, and trade-secret law as sufficient alternatives. If less-restrictive alternatives exist, they undercut justification for non-compete exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of in terrorem effects from case-by-case adjudication
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether leaving enforceability to case-by-case litigation would chill competition and undermine rule objectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case-by-case adjudication can produce in terrorem effects—threatening litigation risk deters worker mobility and undermines certainty. Broad exceptions that prompt fact-specific litigation would materially weaken the rule's aim to reduce non-competes' chilling effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pecuniary benefit to firms is not a cognizable justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether employers may defend non-competes on the ground they produce pecuniary benefits to the firm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under section 5 analysis, firms may not justify an unfair method of competition solely based on pecuniary benefit to themselves; the Commission requires demonstration of societal benefits, not just firm profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of bargaining power and coercion
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of whether non-competes are exploitative/coercive given worker bargaining positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission finds many non-competes (including for highly paid or skilled non-senior-executives) are exploitative/coercive because workers rarely negotiate meaningful consideration, are induced to sign after starting, or face unequal bargaining positions—this weighs against exemptions.
